claim: The mushroom body (MB) in Drosophila is comprised of approximately 2000 Kenyon cells that converge onto 34 output neurons (MBONs) of 21 types.
source: Sensory stimuli are sparsely represented by ∼2000 Kenyon cells, which converge onto 34 output neurons (MBONs) of 21 types.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by anatomical characterization described in the accompanying manuscript (Aso et al., 2014).

claim: Optogenetic activation of MBONs can induce either repulsion or attraction in flies depending on cell type.
source: We also show that optogenetic activation of MBONs can, depending on cell type, induce repulsion or attraction in flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, where CsChrimson activation of different MBON types resulted in either avoidance or attraction behaviors.

claim: The behavioral effects of MBON perturbation are combinatorial.
source: The behavioral effects of MBON perturbation are combinatorial, suggesting that the MBON ensemble collectively represents valence.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 4 where combinations of MBON drivers were tested and showed additive or intermediate effects.

claim: Local, stimulus-specific dopaminergic modulation selectively alters the balance within the MBON network for those stimuli.
source: We propose that local, stimulus-specific dopaminergic modulation selectively alters the balance within the MBON network for those stimuli.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of anatomical and behavioral data, representing an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Valence encoded by the MBON ensemble biases memory-based action selection.
source: Our results suggest that valence encoded by the MBON ensemble biases memory-based action selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental results showing that MBON activation biases behavioral choices.

claim: The mushroom body (MB) is the main center of associative memory in insect brains.
source: The mushroom body (MB) is the main center of associative memory in insect brains (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994, Heisenberg et al., 1985; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this role.

claim: In Drosophila, olfactory information is delivered to the MB by projection neurons from approximately 50 antennal lobe glomeruli.
source: In Drosophila, olfactory information is delivered to the MB by projection neurons from each of ∼50 antennal lobe glomeruli (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Jefferis et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2007; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Connections between projection neurons and Kenyon cells are not stereotyped, meaning individual flies show distinct wiring patterns.
source: Connections between the projection neurons and the ∼2000 Kenyon cells (KCs), the neurons whose parallel axonal fibers form the MB lobes (Crittenden et al., 1998; Aso et al., 2009), are not stereotyped (Figure 1A) (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013); that is, individual flies show distinct wiring patterns between projection neurons and KCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: Sparse activity of Kenyon cells represents the identity of odors.
source: Sparse activity of the KCs represents the identity of odors (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Turner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior physiological studies.

claim: The output of the MB is conveyed to the rest of the brain by 34 cells of 21 cell types per brain hemisphere.
source: The output of the MB is conveyed to the rest of the brain by a remarkably small number of neurons—34 cells of 21 cell types per brain hemisphere (Figure 1B, Table 1) (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data presented in the accompanying manuscript and shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: The innervation patterns of extrinsic neurons define 15 compartments in the MB lobes and one compartment in the core of distal pedunculus.
source: The innervation patterns of extrinsic neurons define 15 compartments in the MB lobes and one compartment in the core of distal pedunculus (pedc)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the accompanying manuscript.

claim: MBONs using the same neurotransmitter are spatially co-localized in the lobes.
source: MBONs using the same transmitter are spatially co-localized in the lobes (See Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B where MBONs are color-coded by neurotransmitter type and their spatial organization is depicted.

claim: Activation of subsets of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) can substitute for reinforcing stimuli to induce either appetitive or aversive memory.
source: Moreover, exogenous activation of these DANs can substitute for reinforcing stimuli to induce either appetitive or aversive memory, depending on DAN cell type (Figure 1A) (Yamagata et al., in press, Perisse et al., 2013; Schroll et al., 2006; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010, 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies and indicated in Figure 1A.

claim: D1-like dopamine receptors and components of the cAMP signaling pathway are required specifically in Kenyon cells for memory formation.
source: D1-like dopamine receptors and components of the cAMP signaling pathway, such as the Ca2+/Calmodulin-responsive adenylate cyclase encoded by the rutabaga gene, are required specifically in the KCs for memory formation (Livingstone et al., 1984; Zars et al., 2000; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2003; Gervasi et al., 2010; Qin et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior molecular and genetic studies.

claim: Reward and punishment recruit distinct sets of dopaminergic neurons that project to specific regions in the MB lobes.
source: Reward and punishment recruit distinct sets of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) that project to specific regions in the MB lobes (Mao and Davis, 2009; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: All MBONs eliciting aversion were glutamatergic and all MBONs eliciting attraction were either GABAergic or cholinergic.
source: Behavioral valence was highly correlated with MBON transmitter type: all MBONs eliciting aversion were glutamatergic and all the MBONs eliciting attraction were either GABAergic or cholinergic.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Activating sensory neurons for CO2 or bitter taste induced strong avoidance in the behavioral valence assay.
source: Activating sensory neurons for CO2 or bitter taste in this manner induced strong avoidance (Figure 2B), consistent with previous reports (Suh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to a prior study.

claim: Co-activation of MBON cell types with opposing effects resulted in intermediate responses.
source: Conversely, co-activation of MBON cell types with opposing effects resulted in intermediate responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When combining drivers eliciting similar responses, flies generally showed a stronger response than to either driver alone.
source: When combining drivers eliciting similar responses, flies generally showed a stronger response than to either driver alone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: MBON activity biases the direction that flies turn in the choice zone, thereby biasing the direction in which they exit that zone.
source: Our results indicate that MBON activity biases the direction that flies turn in the choice zone, thereby biasing the direction in which they exit that zone.
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was little correlation between preference index and either mean walking speed or mean angular velocity of flies in illuminated quadrants.
source: In contrast, we found little correlation between preference index and either mean walking speed or mean angular velocity, an indicator of turning probability, of flies in illuminated quadrants (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Flies did not display a stereotyped turning behavior in the choice zones.
source: We did not observe a stereotyped turning behavior in the choice zones; more specifically, the time between entering the choice zone and making a turn as well as the precise direction of the turn varied (Figure 5E; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by the trajectory data shown in Figure 5E and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: MBONs represent valence, abstract information that serves to bias rather than direct specific motor patterns.
source: These observations support the view that MBONs represent valence, abstract information that serves to bias—rather than direct—specific motor patterns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral observations showing variable motor patterns in response to MBON activation.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc dopaminergic neuron plays a central role in formation of aversive memory in both olfactory and visual learning paradigms.
source: Consistent with this large body of work, we found that one type of PPL1 cluster DAN, PPL1-γ1pedc, played a central role in formation of aversive memory in both olfactory (Figure 6; see also Aso et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2010) and visual learning (Figure 8) paradigms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 8, as well as citations to prior studies.

claim: Blocking MBON-γ1pedc>α/β impaired both short-term aversive odor and visual memory.
source: For example, we found that blocking MBON-γ1pedc>α/β impaired both short-term aversive odor and visual memory, suggesting a general role in aversive memory independent of modality.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: A subset of glutamatergic MBONs was required in all three appetitive memory assays.
source: Conversely, a subset of glutamatergic MBONs was required in all three appetitive memory assays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7, 9, and 11.

claim: Inactivation of MB052B, which broadly labels cholinergic V2 cluster MBONs, resulted in nearly complete loss of aversive odor long-term memory recall.
source: Inactivation of MB052B, which broadly labels cholinergic V2 cluster MBONs (Figure 3F; Table 1), resulted in nearly complete loss of aversive odor LTM recall (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: V2 cluster MBONs function as a group in the retrieval of aversive odor long-term memory.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that V2 cluster MBONs (Figure 10D) function as a group in the retrieval of aversive odor LTM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking subsets of V2 MBONs individually did not show significant impairment, but blocking them together did.

claim: Flies are able to associate an odor with the intoxicating properties of ethanol.
source: Flies are able to associate an odor with the intoxicating properties of ethanol (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental paradigm described and data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Flies avoid the odor they experienced at the time of intoxication when tested 30 min after training, but show a long-lasting preference for that odor when tested 24 or more hours later.
source: Flies avoid the odor they experienced at the time of intoxication when tested 30 min after training, but show a long-lasting preference for that odor when tested 24 or more hours later (control data in Figure 11B,C) (Kaun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 11B and 11C, and a citation to a prior study.

claim: Silencing MBON-α′2 resulted in persistence of the aversive memory after 24 hr, when control flies show appetitive memory.
source: Silencing MBON-α′2, a cell type composed of just one cell in each hemisphere (Figure 11—figure supplement 1F,G) (Aso et al., 2014), resulted in persistence of the aversive memory after 24 hr, when control flies show appetitive memory (see MB018B in Figure 11D and MB091C in Figure 12E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 11D and 11E (referenced as 12E in the text, likely a typo).

claim: Maintenance of the aversive memory upon inactivation of MBON-α′2 argues against a passive dissipation of the aversive memory with time, and implies an active process in the conversion of aversive to appetitive memory.
source: Moreover, maintenance of the aversive memory upon inactivation of MBON-α′2 argues against a passive dissipation of the aversive memory with time, and implies an active process in the conversion of aversive to appetitive memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that blocking MBON-α′2 prevents the switch from aversive to appetitive memory.

claim: Five MBON drivers suppressed sleep when activated with dTrpA1.
source: We identified five MBON drivers that suppressed sleep and seven MBON drivers that increased sleep (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Seven MBON drivers increased sleep when activated with dTrpA1.
source: We identified five MBON drivers that suppressed sleep and seven MBON drivers that increased sleep (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: All five sleep-suppressing drivers express in glutamatergic MBONs.
source: All five sleep-suppressing drivers express in glutamatergic MBONs (MBON-γ5β′2a, MBON-β′2mp, MBON-β′2a_bilateral and MBON-γ4>γ1γ2), while sleep-promoting drivers express either in GABAergic (MBON-γ3β′1 and MBON-γ3) or cholinergic MBONs (MBON-γ2α′1); the neurotransmitter for MBON-calyx has not been determined (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12B and anatomical characterization.

claim: Sleep-promoting drivers express either in GABAergic or cholinergic MBONs.
source: All five sleep-suppressing drivers express in glutamatergic MBONs (MBON-γ5β′2a, MBON-β′2mp, MBON-β′2a_bilateral and MBON-γ4>γ1γ2), while sleep-promoting drivers express either in GABAergic (MBON-γ3β′1 and MBON-γ3) or cholinergic MBONs (MBON-γ2α′1); the neurotransmitter for MBON-calyx has not been determined (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12B and anatomical characterization.

claim: The subset of MBONs that promoted sleep was similar to the subset in which CsChrimson activation was attractive.
source: The subset of MBONs that promoted sleep was similar to the subset in which CsChrimson activation was attractive; conversely, the MBON subset that promoted wakefulness was similar to the subset in which CsChrimson activation was aversive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the results of the sleep assays (Figure 12) with the valence assays (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: The MBON subset that promoted wakefulness was similar to the subset in which CsChrimson activation was aversive.
source: The subset of MBONs that promoted sleep was similar to the subset in which CsChrimson activation was attractive; conversely, the MBON subset that promoted wakefulness was similar to the subset in which CsChrimson activation was aversive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the results of the sleep assays (Figure 12) with the valence assays (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: The axons of the sleep promoting cholinergic MBON-γ2α′1 and wake promoting glutamatergic MBON-β′2mp project their termini to the same location in the brain.
source: For example, the axons of the sleep promoting cholinergic MBON-γ2α′1 and wake promoting glutamatergic MBON-β′2mp project their termini to the same location in the brain (Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Video 6.

claim: A sparse and non-stereotyped ensemble of Kenyon cells represents environmental cues such as odors.
source: In the insect brain, a sparse and non-stereotyped ensemble of Kenyon cells represents environmental cues such as odors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: MBONs are thought to encode the predictive value associated with a stimulus.
source: MBONs are thought to encode the predictive value associated with a stimulus.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of anatomical and behavioral data.

claim: Activation of glutamatergic MBONs repelled flies and promoted wakefulness.
source: Activation of glutamatergic MBONs repelled flies and promoted wakefulness, whereas activation of GABAergic or cholinergic MBONs attracted flies and promoted sleep.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 12.

claim: Activation of GABAergic or cholinergic MBONs attracted flies and promoted sleep.
source: Activation of glutamatergic MBONs repelled flies and promoted wakefulness, whereas activation of GABAergic or cholinergic MBONs attracted flies and promoted sleep.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 12.

claim: More cell types were involved in appetitive memory than in aversive memory.
source: In general, more cell types were involved in appetitive memory than in aversive memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the results across different memory assays shown in Figures 6-11 and summarized in Figure 13.

claim: Partially overlapping sets of cholinergic and glutamatergic MBONs were required for all three appetitive memory assays.
source: Partially overlapping set of cholinergic and glutamatergic MBONs were required for all three appetitive memory assays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7, 9, and 11, and summarized in Figure 13.

claim: The same GABAergic MBON-γ1pedc>α/β was required for short-term olfactory and visual memory.
source: The same GABAergic MBON-γ1pedc>α/β was required for short-term olfactory and visual memory in an assay protocol that did not distinguish between formation or retrieval
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Long-term aversive odor memory retrieval required the V2 cluster MBONs.
source: whereas long-term aversive odor memory retrieval required the V2 cluster MBONs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Flies can move and orient themselves when MBONs are inactivated with Shibire.
source: Thus flies can move and orient themselves when MBONs, and any neurons with off-target expression in these split-GAL4 drivers, are inactivated and the small differences from wild-type would not be expected to significantly affect behavior in the assays we performed that used Shibire as an effector.
evidence: This is based on the results of control experiments assessing innate behaviors.

claim: Activation of PPL1-γ1pedc dopaminergic neurons can substitute for electric shock as the unconditioned stimulus.
source: Activation of the PPL1-γ1pedc dopaminergic neurons can substitute for electric shock as the unconditioned stimulus (US). Flies trained using thermoactivation of MB438B/dTrpA1 as the US showed robust 3 min aversive memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: MBON-γ1pedc>α/β is immunoreactive to GABA.
source: MBON-γ1pedc>α/β is immunoreactive to GABA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MBON-γ1pedc>α/β is one of only three MBON cell types with axon terminals within the MB lobes.
source: and is one of only three MBON cell types with axon terminals within the MB lobes (Figure 6H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E) (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E, and cited from the accompanying manuscript.

claim: The axon terminals of PPL1-γ1pedc DAN precisely overlap with the dendrites of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β in the MB pedunculus and γ1 compartment.
source: We visualized the single-cell morphologies of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (Figure 6I) and PPL1-γ1pedc (Figure 6J) and using two-color labeling confirmed that the axon terminals of the DAN (one or two cells per brain hemisphere) precisely overlap with the dendrites of the MBON (a single cell per brain hemisphere) in the MB pedunculus and γ1 compartment (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 6I, 6J, and 6K.

claim: PAM cluster DANs that innervate the compartments of glutamatergic MBONs are sufficient to induce appetitive memory.
source: For appetitive memory, PAM cluster DANs that innervate other regions of the MB lobes, in particular the compartments of glutamatergic MBONs, are sufficient to induce appetitive memory (Yamagata et al., in press) (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) (Perisse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The sign of preference observed in response to CsChrimson activation of particular MBONs was, in general, opposite to that of the memory induced by dopaminergic input to the corresponding MB compartments.
source: The sign of preference we observed in response to CsChrimson activation of particular MBONs was, in general, opposite to that of the memory induced by dopaminergic input to the corresponding MB compartments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the results of MBON activation (Figures 2-3) with the known effects of DAN activation on memory formation.

claim: Activation of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β and MBON-γ2α′1 attracted flies, whereas DAN input to these regions induced aversive memory.
source: For example, activation of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β and MBON-γ2α′1 attracted flies (Figure 2), whereas DAN input to these regions induced aversive memory (Figure 6G) (Aso et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 6G, and citations to prior studies.

claim: Activation of glutamatergic MBONs repelled flies, while DAN input to the corresponding regions is known to induce appetitive memory.
source: Conversely, activation of glutamatergic MBONs repelled flies (Figure 2), while DAN input to the corresponding regions is known to induce appetitive memory (Yamagata et al., in press) (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) (Perisse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to prior studies.

claim: These results are most easily explained if dopamine modulation led to synaptic depression of the outputs of the KCs representing the CS+ stimulus.
source: These results are most easily explained if dopamine modulation led to synaptic depression of the outputs of the KCs representing the CS + stimulus.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The PE1 MBONs in honeybees reduce their response to a learned odor.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, the PE1 MBONs in honeybees (Okada et al., 2007) as well as the V2 cluster MBONs in Drosophila (Sejourne et al., 2011) reduce their response to a learned odor
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior physiological studies.

claim: The V2 cluster MBONs in Drosophila reduce their response to a learned odor.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, the PE1 MBONs in honeybees (Okada et al., 2007) as well as the V2 cluster MBONs in Drosophila (Sejourne et al., 2011) reduce their response to a learned odor
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior physiological study.

claim: Depression of KC-MBON synapses has been shown for octopamine modulation in the locust MB.
source: and depression of KC-MBON synapses has been shown for octopamine modulation in the locust MB (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Long-term synaptic depression occurs in the granular cell synapses to Purkinje cells in the vertebrate cerebellum.
source: Moreover, long-term synaptic depression is known to occur in the granular cell synapses to Purkinje cells in the vertebrate cerebellum (Ito et al., 1982), a local neuronal circuit with many analogies to the MB (Schurmann, 1974; Laurent, 2002; Farris, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The DANs and MBONs mediating aversive memory innervate the same regions of MB lobes.
source: In the cases described above, the DANs and MBONs mediating a particular behavior innervate the same regions of MB lobes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical and behavioral data presented.

claim: The compartments with cholinergic MBONs do not receive inputs from reward-mediating PAM cluster DANs.
source: For example, even though several cholinergic MBONs are required for appetitive memory (Placais et al., 2013), the compartments with cholinergic MBONs do not receive inputs from reward-mediating PAM cluster DANs, but instead from PPL1 cluster DANs that have been shown to be dispensable for odor-sugar memory (Schwaerzel et al., 2003) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior studies.

claim: CsChrimson activation of the cholinergic MBON-γ2α′1 and V2 cluster MBONs resulted in attraction.
source: But the fact that CsChrimson activation of the cholinergic MBON-γ2α′1 and V2 cluster MBONs resulted in attraction, strongly suggests that at least some of the cholinergic MBONs have a role in directly mediating the conditioned response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Previous studies found a requirement for cholinergic MBONs during memory retrieval.
source: Indeed, previous studies found a requirement for cholinergic MBONs (the V2 cluster and MBON-α3) during memory retrieval (Sejourne et al., 2011; Pai et al., 2013; Placais et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The multilayered arrangement of MBONs provides a circuit mechanism that enables local modulation in one compartment to affect the response of MBONs in other compartments.
source: The multilayered arrangement of MBONs (see Figure 17 of the accompanying manuscript) (Aso et al., 2014) provides a circuit mechanism that enables local modulation in one compartment to affect the response of MBONs in other compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization described in the accompanying manuscript.

claim: The avoidance-mediating MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 targets the compartments of attraction-mediating MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β.
source: For example, the avoidance-mediating MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 targets the compartments of attraction-mediating MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (Figure 14).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 14.

claim: Circuits in the α lobe play key roles in long-term aversive and appetitive memory.
source: Previous studies and our results indicate that circuits in the α lobe play key roles in long-term aversive and appetitive memory (Figure 10) (Pascual and Preat, 2001; Isabel et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2006; Blum et al., 2009; Sejourne et al., 2011; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2013; Placais et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 and citations to prior studies.

claim: The α lobe is targeted by MBONs from other compartments and comprises the last layer in the layered output model of the MB.
source: The α lobe is targeted by MBONs from other compartments and comprises the last layer in the layered output model of the MB (Figure 1B; see also Figure 17 of the accompanying manuscript) (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1B and cited from the accompanying manuscript.

claim: The GABAergic MBON-γ1pedc>α/β and the glutamatergic MBON-β1>α both project to α2 and α3, where their axonal termini lie in close apposition.
source: The GABAergic MBON-γ1pedc>α/β and the glutamatergic MBON-β1>α both project to α2 and α3, where their axonal termini lie in close apposition (see Figure 17 of the accompanying manuscript) (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data cited from the accompanying manuscript.

claim: DAN input to the compartments housing the dendrites of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β and MBON-β1>α induces aversive and appetitive memory, respectively.
source: DAN input to the compartments housing the dendrites of these feedforward MBONs induces aversive and appetitive memory, respectively (this work) (Perisse et al., 2013; Yamagata et al., in press).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from this study and citations to prior studies.

claim: Neurons that are thought to mediate innate response to odors also project to the same convergence zones as MBONs.
source: Neurons that are thought to mediate innate response to odors—a subset of projection neurons from the antennal lobes and output neurons from the lateral horn—also project to these same convergence zones (Figure 15; Figure 15—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 15 and Figure 15—figure supplement 1.

claim: These convergence zones serve as network nodes where behavioral output is selected in the light of both the innate and learned valences of stimuli.
source: We propose that these convergence zones serve as network nodes where behavioral output is selected in the light of both the innate and learned valences of stimuli.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the anatomical observations.

claim: Neurons that project to the fan-shaped body of the central complex have dendrites that widely arborize in the same areas as MBON terminals.
source: One obvious possibility is neurons that project to the fan-shaped body of the central complex whose dendrites are known to widely arborize in these same areas (Hanesch et al., 1989; Young and Armstrong, 2010a; Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The failure to see effects when inactivating individual cell types is most easily explained by combinatorial roles and redundancy between MBONs.
source: The failure to see effects when inactivating individual cell types is most easily explained by combinatorial roles and redundancy between MBONs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that some expected phenotypes were not detected.

claim: The MB is implicated in functions beyond processing of associative memory.
source: The MBs are implicated in functions beyond processing of associative memory (Martin et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1999; Joiner et al., 2006; Pitman et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007; Hong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: MBONs that influence approach to, or avoidance of, a learned stimulus may also have roles in innate preference behaviors for temperature and hunger-dependent CO2 avoidance.
source: MBONs that influence approach to, or avoidance of, a learned stimulus may also have roles in innate preference behaviors for temperature and hunger-dependent CO2 avoidance (Hong et al., 2008; Bang et al., 2011; Bracker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known roles of the MB and citations to prior studies.

claim: The MB is known to play a role in experience-dependent regulation of proboscis extension and courtship as well as regulation of sleep and post-mating behaviors such as oviposition.
source: Moreover, we expect the behavioral repertoire that MBONs govern to go beyond simple approach and avoidance; the MB is known to play a role in experience-dependent regulation of proboscis extension (Masek and Scott, 2010) and courtship (McBride et al., 1999) as well as regulation of sleep (Joiner et al., 2006; Pitman et al., 2006) and post-mating behaviors such as oviposition (Fleischmann et al., 2001; Azanchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The diverse influences of MBONs on behavior can be most easily explained if the activity of the ensemble of MBONs conveys an abstract representation of both valence and internal state.
source: The diverse influences of MBONs on behavior can be most easily explained if we assume that the activity of the ensemble of MBON conveys an abstract representation of both valence and internal state.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of all the behavioral observations.

claim: The ensemble of MBONs may represent internal states along axes such as pleasant-unpleasant or aroused-not aroused.
source: In this view, the ensemble of MBONs may represent internal states along axes such as pleasant-unpleasant or aroused-not aroused.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Primitive forms of emotion are thought to have evolved along axes such as pleasant-unpleasant or aroused-not aroused.
source: It is upon these axes that primitive forms of emotion are thought to have evolved (Anderson and Adolphs, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior theoretical work.
